topics.topic: Audit data analytics and IT considerations

questions.q: An auditor uses a data analytics tool to compare 100% of a client's sales invoices to shipping records and identifies 14 invoices with no matching shipment. Which of the following is the auditor's most appropriate next step?
choices: Conclude that revenue is fairly stated because every item in the population was tested
Treat the exceptions as clearly trivial because they were identified by an automated tool
Investigate the 14 exceptions to determine whether they represent misstatements or control deficiencies
Project the 14 exceptions to the population using a statistical sampling formula
questions.exp: Items flagged by an audit data analytic are exceptions that require follow-up to determine their nature and cause before the auditor can conclude. Projection is a sampling concept and is unnecessary when the full population was examined; the exceptions themselves are the known items to evaluate.

questions.q: Before relying on a client-generated report of accounts receivable aging as input to an analytical procedure, the auditor should primarily obtain evidence about which of the following?
choices: Whether the report format agrees with the prior-year report
Whether management has reviewed and signed the report
Whether the report was prepared by someone independent of the credit function
The accuracy and completeness of the information in the report
questions.exp: AU-C 500 requires the auditor to evaluate whether information produced by the entity is sufficiently reliable, including obtaining evidence about its accuracy and completeness. Management sign-off or consistent formatting does not establish that the underlying data is complete and accurate.

questions.q: An auditor plans to rely on an automated three-way match control in the client's ERP system. The auditor tested the control in the prior year. Which of the following would best support a benchmarking strategy that reduces testing of the automated control this year?
choices: Effective IT general controls over program changes confirm the control has not been changed since it was last tested
The control has been in place for more than three years
Management represents in writing that the control operated effectively all year
The auditor tested a sample of manual journal entries and found no errors
questions.exp: An automated control will continue to perform consistently unless the program is changed, so benchmarking depends on effective general IT controls (especially change management) showing the control is unchanged. A management representation is not sufficient evidence of operating effectiveness.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a general IT control rather than an application control?
choices: An automated recalculation of invoice extensions
An edit check rejecting a sales order with an invalid customer number
Restricting access to production programs to authorized IT personnel
A batch total comparison of hours input to hours processed in payroll
questions.exp: General IT controls apply to the IT environment broadly, such as access security, program change, and IT operations. Edit checks, batch totals, and automated calculations operate within a specific application over specific transactions and are application controls.

questions.q: Under AU-C 315 (as clarified by SAS No. 145), how should an auditor approach the identification of general IT controls?
choices: Identify IT applications and aspects of the IT environment subject to risks arising from IT, then identify general IT controls that address those risks
Test all general IT controls in every audit regardless of planned reliance on controls
Identify general IT controls only for public entities subject to PCAOB standards
Identify general IT controls only when the client uses a service organization
questions.exp: SAS 145 requires the auditor to identify the IT applications and other aspects of the IT environment that are subject to risks arising from the use of IT, and then the related general IT controls that address those risks. It does not require testing all general IT controls in every audit.

questions.q: An auditor uses an audit data analytic to recalculate depreciation for every fixed asset in the population and finds no differences above a small threshold. The analytic is best characterized as which type of procedure?
choices: A test of controls over the fixed asset subledger
A risk assessment procedure only
A substantive procedure that may provide evidence about valuation of depreciation expense
A walkthrough of the fixed asset process
questions.exp: Recalculation of depreciation for the population is a substantive test of details that provides direct evidence about the amounts recorded. It does not test whether a control operated, and it goes beyond risk assessment because it is designed to detect material misstatement.

questions.q: A client outsources payroll processing to a service organization. The user auditor intends to rely on controls at the service organization. Which report would most directly support that reliance?
choices: A SOC 3 report intended for general use
A SOC 1 Type 2 report on the description, design, and operating effectiveness of controls over a period
A SOC 1 Type 1 report describing the design of controls at a point in time
A SOC 2 Type 2 report on security and availability controls
questions.exp: Under AU-C 402, reliance on operating effectiveness requires evidence over a period, which a Type 2 report on controls relevant to financial reporting (SOC 1) provides. A Type 1 report addresses design and implementation only, and SOC 2/SOC 3 address trust services criteria rather than internal control over financial reporting.

questions.q: A SOC 1 Type 2 report states that the service organization's controls are effective only if user entities implement certain complementary user entity controls. What should the user auditor do?
choices: Ignore the complementary controls because the service auditor already tested them
Evaluate whether the user entity has designed and implemented the complementary user entity controls and, if relying on them, test them
Modify the opinion for a scope limitation
Request that the service auditor extend testing to the user entity
questions.exp: Complementary user entity controls are the user entity's responsibility, so the user auditor must consider them at the user entity (AU-C 402). The service auditor does not test controls at user entities, which is the trap in assuming they are already covered.

questions.q: An auditor uses software to stratify the accounts payable population and select all vendors with balances above a threshold plus a sample of the remainder. The software is most appropriately described as being used to:
choices: Evaluate the operating effectiveness of IT general controls
Replace the need for confirmation or other substantive procedures
Assess control risk at the maximum
Select items for testing
questions.exp: Stratification and selection of key items is a selection technique; the selected items still must be tested with substantive procedures. Using software to select items does not itself provide evidence about controls or eliminate further testing.

questions.q: When an auditor's data analytic is applied to the full population of journal entries and produces a large number of items meeting the criteria, which of the following responses is most appropriate?
choices: Select a haphazard sample of the flagged items and conclude on the rest without further consideration
Discard the analytic and revert to traditional sampling
Report all flagged items to those charged with governance as significant deficiencies
Refine the criteria or further disaggregate the results to identify the items that represent a higher risk of misstatement and investigate those
questions.exp: When an analytic produces many 'false positives,' the auditor typically refines the expectation or criteria to isolate notable items that warrant investigation. Flagged items are not automatically control deficiencies, and abandoning the analytic ignores useful evidence.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of an integrated test facility (ITF)?
choices: To monitor online transactions continuously by embedding audit modules
To extract data from client files for analysis on the auditor's computer
To process fictitious auditor transactions through the client's live system alongside actual transactions and compare results to expectations
To compare two versions of a program to detect unauthorized changes
questions.exp: An ITF creates a dummy entity in the live system so auditor test data is processed with real data, testing processing controls. Generalized audit software extracts and analyzes data, and parallel simulation or code comparison addresses different objectives.

questions.q: An auditor reprocesses actual client payroll data using the auditor's own program and compares the output to the client's payroll register. This technique is:
choices: Parallel simulation
Test data
Embedded audit module
Integrated test facility
questions.exp: Parallel simulation uses the auditor's software to reprocess real client data and compare results. Test data and ITF instead run auditor-created transactions through the client's programs.

questions.q: Which risk arising from IT is most directly addressed by effective segregation between program development and production environments?
choices: Inaccurate data entry by end users
Failure of the client to respond timely to customer inquiries
Unauthorized changes to programs that process financial data
Data loss from inadequate backup procedures
questions.exp: Separating development from production, with controlled migration, addresses the risk that unauthorized or untested program changes reach the systems that process transactions. Backup and data entry risks are addressed by other controls.

questions.q: An entity's sales application allows a sales manager to both create new customers and override credit limits. Which IT-related deficiency does this most directly represent?
choices: Inadequate logical access controls that fail to enforce segregation of duties
An ineffective program change process
A data conversion error
Inadequate backup and recovery
questions.exp: Access rights that let one user perform incompatible functions reflect a logical access/segregation of duties deficiency. Program change and backup controls address different risks.

questions.q: An auditor uses an audit data analytic during planning to compare monthly gross margin by product line to prior years and industry data. The primary purpose of this analytic is to:
choices: Test the operating effectiveness of revenue controls
Satisfy the requirement for an overall review near the end of the audit
Provide sufficient appropriate evidence to support the opinion on revenue
Identify unusual relationships that may indicate risks of material misstatement
questions.exp: Analytical procedures used as risk assessment procedures (AU-C 315, AU-C 520) help identify unusual relationships that may indicate risks. A planning analytic alone is generally not designed to provide substantive evidence sufficient to support conclusions.

questions.q: When using an analytic as a substantive analytical procedure under AU-C 520, which of the following is required?
choices: The difference must be investigated only if it exceeds overall materiality
The auditor must develop an expectation precise enough to identify a misstatement that could be material and determine the acceptable difference
The auditor must test 100% of the population
The expectation must be developed by the client's management
questions.exp: AU-C 520 requires the auditor to develop a sufficiently precise expectation from reliable data and determine the amount of difference that is acceptable without further investigation. The threshold is usually set below overall materiality, and the expectation should be the auditor's, not management's.

questions.q: An auditor uses an AI-enabled tool provided by the firm to analyze lease contracts. Under the firm's quality management system, which statement is most accurate?
choices: Output of firm-approved tools need not be documented
The engagement team remains responsible for determining that the tool is appropriate for the engagement and for evaluating its output
Using the tool shifts responsibility for the conclusions to the tool vendor
Because the firm approved the tool, the engagement team may accept its output without evaluation
questions.exp: Under SQMS 1 and the engagement-level standards, firm-approved technological resources still require the engagement team to use them appropriately and exercise professional judgment over their output. Firm approval does not remove the team's responsibility or documentation requirements.

questions.q: An auditor identified that the client's password parameters were weak but tested and found effective compensating controls over user access reviews. The auditor's most appropriate conclusion regarding automated application controls that depend on access security is:
choices: Reliance on the automated controls may still be appropriate if the compensating controls address the risk
The auditor must perform a 100% test of all transactions
Automated controls cannot be relied upon under any circumstances
The auditor must issue an adverse opinion on the financial statements
questions.exp: A general IT control deficiency requires the auditor to evaluate its effect, and effective compensating controls can mitigate the risk so reliance on dependent application controls may remain appropriate. An IT deficiency does not automatically preclude reliance or affect the opinion on the financial statements.

questions.q: An auditor extracts the client's entire general ledger and uses software to identify journal entries posted on weekends, by unusual users, or with round-dollar amounts. These procedures most directly respond to which requirement?
choices: Confirming balances with third parties
Evaluating going concern
Obtaining an understanding of the entity's industry
Testing the appropriateness of journal entries to address the risk of management override of controls
questions.exp: AU-C 240 requires procedures to test journal entries and other adjustments for management override; analytics that identify entries with fraud-risk characteristics are a common approach. The other procedures address different audit objectives.

questions.q: Which of the following attributes of data is most important when an auditor evaluates the reliability of external data (for example, an industry price index) used in an analytic?
choices: Whether the data was purchased rather than obtained free
The source's competence and objectivity, and whether the data is relevant to the assertion
Whether management prefers the source
Whether the data is presented in the same format as the client's records
questions.exp: Under AU-C 500 (as amended by SAS 142), the auditor considers the relevance and reliability of information, including the source's competence, objectivity, and any bias. Format, cost, or management preference do not determine reliability.

questions.q: An auditor's analytic compares the dates of shipment on the shipping log to invoice dates for all sales near year-end. This analytic primarily provides evidence about which assertion?
choices: Rights and obligations
Presentation
Cutoff
Valuation
questions.exp: Comparing shipment dates to invoice dates around period-end tests whether sales are recorded in the proper period, which is the cutoff assertion. It does not address valuation of receivables or ownership.

questions.q: The use of cloud computing by a client most directly affects the auditor's understanding of which of the following?
choices: The entity's IT environment, including reliance on third-party providers and related controls
The determination of overall materiality
The applicable financial reporting framework
The auditor's independence
questions.exp: Cloud hosting means a third party performs IT functions, so the auditor considers the IT environment, risks arising from IT, and whether service organization reporting (for example, a SOC 1) is needed. Cloud use does not change the reporting framework or materiality.

questions.q: For which of the following would a test of an automated control typically require the smallest sample, assuming effective general IT controls?
choices: A manual control performed daily
An automated control, which can often be tested with one or a few instances
A manual control performed weekly
A manual review control performed quarterly
questions.exp: Because automated controls perform consistently when general IT controls are effective, a test of one or a few instances can suffice. Manual controls are subject to human error, so sample sizes depend on frequency and are larger.

questions.q: An auditor wants evidence that all approved credit memos were recorded. Using a data analytic, the auditor should compare:
choices: The approved credit memo file to recorded credit memos in the sales returns journal
Recorded credit memos in the sales returns journal to the approved credit memo file
Recorded credit memos to the shipping log
Customer remittances to the cash receipts journal
questions.exp: Completeness is tested by tracing from source documents (approved credit memos) to the accounting records. Tracing from the journal back to documents tests occurrence, which is the reversed-direction trap.

questions.q: In an integrated audit under PCAOB AS 2201, the auditor's evaluation of IT includes which of the following?
choices: Issuing a separate opinion on the effectiveness of the entity's IT security
Testing every IT general control at the entity regardless of relevance to financial reporting
Understanding how IT affects the flow of transactions and identifying risks arising from IT that relate to relevant assertions
Relying on the client's IT department testing without evaluation
questions.exp: AS 2201 requires the auditor to understand IT's effect on the flow of transactions and to address risks arising from IT that are relevant to ICFR. It does not require testing irrelevant IT controls or a separate IT security opinion.

questions.q: A client converted to a new general ledger system mid-year. Which procedure most directly addresses the risk of misstatement from the conversion?
choices: Test controls over data conversion, such as reconciliations of balances transferred from the old system to the new system
Increase overall materiality because the new system is more reliable
Review the vendor's marketing material about the system
Inquire of IT about user satisfaction with the new system
questions.exp: Data conversion creates a risk that balances are incompletely or inaccurately transferred, so the auditor tests conversion controls or reconciles balances. User satisfaction and vendor claims provide no evidence about transferred data.

questions.q: An auditor identifies a significant risk of revenue recognition and plans to address it only with a substantive analytical procedure using disaggregated data. Under AU-C 330, which is correct?
choices: This is never acceptable for revenue
This is acceptable only if the auditor also obtains a management representation
This is acceptable because analytics provide stronger evidence than tests of details
When the approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, those procedures must include tests of details
questions.exp: AU-C 330 requires that if the response to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, it must include tests of details. Analytics alone are insufficient in that case; a representation letter does not substitute.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of evidence that the auditor has addressed the reliability of data used in an audit data analytic?
choices: The analytic produced results consistent with the auditor's expectation
The auditor reconciled the extracted data's record counts and totals to the general ledger and tested relevant controls over the data
The data was provided in a spreadsheet
The client's IT manager confirmed the data was extracted correctly
questions.exp: Reconciling extracted data to the ledger and testing controls over its generation provide evidence of completeness and accuracy (AU-C 500). Results matching expectations can be circular if the data itself is unreliable, and a verbal confirmation is weak evidence.

questions.q: A small client uses off-the-shelf accounting software that does not allow source code modification. How does this most likely affect the auditor's consideration of general IT controls over program changes?
choices: Program change controls must be tested more extensively
The auditor must obtain a SOC 1 Type 2 report from the software vendor
Risks from program changes are likely lower, so fewer program change controls may be relevant
The auditor cannot rely on any automated calculations
questions.exp: When software cannot be modified, the risk of unauthorized program changes is reduced, so the auditor scales the understanding of related general IT controls. Packaged software does not automatically require a vendor SOC 1 report or preclude reliance on automated functionality.

questions.q: An auditor's analytic identifies a vendor whose bank account matches an employee's direct deposit account. This finding most likely indicates a heightened risk of:
choices: Fictitious vendor or disbursement fraud
Understated inventory
Lapping of customer receipts
Improper revenue cutoff
questions.exp: A vendor bank account matching an employee's account is a classic indicator of a fictitious vendor scheme to divert disbursements. Lapping involves customer cash receipts, not vendor payments.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer concludes that inventory is overstated by an amount that is material but not pervasive, and management refuses to adjust. Which opinion should be expressed?
choices: Disclaimer of opinion
Qualified opinion
Adverse opinion
Unmodified opinion with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
questions.exp: Under AU-C 705, a material misstatement that is not pervasive results in a qualified ('except for') opinion. An adverse opinion requires the misstatement to be both material and pervasive, and an emphasis-of-matter paragraph cannot be used to address a misstatement.

questions.q: In an audit report on a nonissuer's financial statements under AU-C 700, which section must appear first?
choices: Key Audit Matters
Responsibilities of Management for the Financial Statements
Opinion
Basis for Opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 700 (as revised by SAS 134) requires the Opinion section to be presented first, followed immediately by the Basis for Opinion section. Key audit matters, when communicated, follow the Basis for Opinion and any going concern section.

questions.q: Before accepting an engagement, the auditor learns that management will prohibit confirmation of receivables and observation of inventory, both of which are material and whose possible effects would be pervasive. No law requires the auditor to accept. What should the auditor do?
choices: Accept and issue a qualified opinion
Accept and perform alternative procedures, then issue an unmodified opinion
Decline the engagement
Accept and issue an adverse opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 210 and AU-C 705 indicate that if management imposes a scope limitation before acceptance that would likely result in a disclaimer, the auditor should not accept the engagement unless required by law or regulation. An adverse opinion addresses misstatements, not scope limitations.

questions.q: An auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about a foreign subsidiary's balances, and the possible effects of undetected misstatements are both material and pervasive. The auditor should express:
choices: An unmodified opinion with an other-matter paragraph
A disclaimer of opinion
A qualified opinion
An adverse opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 705 requires a disclaimer when the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects could be both material and pervasive. An adverse opinion is reserved for misstatements the auditor has actually concluded exist.

questions.q: When the auditor disclaims an opinion on a nonissuer's financial statements, which change to the report is required?
choices: The report is dated as of the original planned completion date
The report expresses an opinion on the components that were audited
The report omits the statement that the auditor believes the evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for an opinion
The report includes a Key Audit Matters section describing the scope limitation
questions.exp: In a disclaimer, the basis section is retitled 'Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion' and the statement that evidence is sufficient and appropriate is omitted (AU-C 705). Piecemeal opinions on components are not permitted when disclaiming on the financial statements as a whole, and KAMs are not communicated.

questions.q: A nonissuer client changes from FIFO to weighted-average cost for inventory, the change is justified and properly accounted for and disclosed, and its effect is material. How should the auditor's report be affected?
choices: Unmodified opinion with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph describing the change in accounting principle
Unmodified opinion with an other-matter paragraph
No reference to the change is required
Qualified opinion for lack of consistency
questions.exp: AU-C 708 requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph when there is a change in accounting principle that has a material effect, even when the change is justified. A qualified opinion would be appropriate only if the change were not in accordance with the framework.

questions.q: An auditor concludes that substantial doubt about a nonissuer's ability to continue as a going concern exists and management's disclosures are adequate. Under AU-C 570, the auditor's report should:
choices: Include an adverse opinion
Include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph titled 'Going Concern'
Include a qualified opinion
Include a separate section with the heading 'Substantial Doubt About the Entity's Ability to Continue as a Going Concern'
questions.exp: AU-C 570 (SAS 132) requires a separate section with that specific heading when substantial doubt exists and disclosures are adequate; the opinion is unmodified. A modified opinion is appropriate only when disclosure is inadequate or the going concern basis is inappropriate.

questions.q: Which of the following matters would most likely be included in an other-matter paragraph rather than an emphasis-of-matter paragraph?
choices: Significant uncertainty about the outcome of litigation, appropriately disclosed
An early application of a new accounting standard with a material effect
A major catastrophe that has had a significant effect on the entity's financial position, appropriately disclosed
The prior-period financial statements were audited by a predecessor auditor whose report is not reissued
questions.exp: An other-matter paragraph addresses matters not presented or disclosed in the financial statements that are relevant to users' understanding of the audit or the report, such as a predecessor auditor's prior-year report (AU-C 706/700). The other items are disclosed matters fundamental to users' understanding, which are emphasis-of-matter subjects.

questions.q: For an audit of a large accelerated filer under PCAOB AS 3101, which of the following is required in the auditor's report?
choices: Communication of critical audit matters, or a statement that there are none
A section describing key audit matters under AU-C 701
A statement of the audit fee
An emphasis-of-matter paragraph for every significant estimate
questions.exp: AS 3101 requires communication of critical audit matters in audits of issuers other than excluded entities (such as EGCs and brokers/dealers), or a statement that the auditor determined there are none. Key audit matters under AU-C 701 apply only when a nonissuer auditor is engaged to communicate them.

questions.q: Which of the following is required in an auditor's report on an issuer's financial statements under PCAOB AS 3101 but is not required in a report under AU-C 700?
choices: A statement that the audit was conducted in accordance with applicable auditing standards
An opinion on whether the financial statements are presented fairly in all material respects
A statement of the year in which the auditor began serving consecutively as the company's auditor
Identification of the financial statements audited
questions.exp: AS 3101 requires a statement of auditor tenure. Both frameworks require a statement about the auditing standards, identification of the statements, and the opinion.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer is engaged to communicate key audit matters. The auditor issues a qualified opinion due to a misstatement of goodwill. How should the goodwill matter be handled?
choices: Describe it in the Key Audit Matters section instead of the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
Describe it in both the Key Audit Matters section and an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
Describe it in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and refer to that section in the Key Audit Matters section rather than describing it as a KAM
Omit it from the report because it is already reflected in the opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 701 states that a matter giving rise to a modified opinion is by nature a key audit matter but is not described in the KAM section; instead the KAM section refers to the basis for qualified opinion section. Communicating a KAM is never a substitute for a modified opinion.

questions.q: An auditor's report on a nonissuer is dated March 10. On March 20, before the report is released, a subsequent event requiring disclosure occurs and is disclosed by management. The auditor performs procedures only on that event. The auditor should:
choices: Dual-date the report, for example 'March 10, except for Note X, as to which the date is March 20'
Leave the report dated March 10 with no reference to the event
Redate the report to March 20 without performing additional procedures
Issue a separate report on the subsequent event
questions.exp: AU-C 560 permits dual dating so that the auditor's responsibility for events after the original date is limited to the specific note. Redating the entire report extends responsibility to all subsequent events and requires procedures through the new date.

questions.q: An auditor's report on comparative financial statements includes an updated opinion on the prior period that differs from the opinion previously expressed. Under AU-C 700, the auditor should:
choices: Omit the prior period from the report
Include the matter only in the management letter
Issue an adverse opinion on the current period
Disclose in an other-matter paragraph the date and type of the previous opinion, the reasons for the different opinion, and that the updated opinion differs
questions.exp: When an updated opinion on prior-period statements differs from the previous opinion, the auditor discloses the reasons in an other-matter paragraph, including the date and type of prior opinion. The current period's opinion is unaffected unless the matter also affects it.

questions.q: A nonissuer omits from its financial statements a disclosure required by GAAP that is material but not pervasive. If practicable, the auditor's report should:
choices: Express an unmodified opinion with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph containing the information
Express a qualified opinion and include the omitted information in the basis for qualified opinion section
Express an adverse opinion and omit the information
Express a disclaimer of opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 705 requires that for omitted required disclosures, the auditor describes the nature of the omitted information and, if practicable and the information is available, includes it in the basis paragraph. The opinion is qualified when material but not pervasive.

questions.q: Required supplementary information (RSI) accompanies a nonissuer's audited financial statements and the auditor applied the limited procedures with no exceptions. The auditor's report should include:
choices: An other-matter paragraph referring to the RSI and stating that limited procedures were applied and no opinion is expressed
An opinion on the RSI in relation to the financial statements as a whole
An emphasis-of-matter paragraph stating the RSI is fairly presented
No reference to RSI
questions.exp: AU-C 730 requires an other-matter paragraph addressing RSI in all cases, stating the limited procedures and that the auditor does not express an opinion. An 'in relation to' opinion applies to supplementary information under AU-C 725, not to RSI.

questions.q: A nonissuer's annual report contains other information (a letter to shareholders) that the auditor obtained before the report date. The auditor read it and found no material inconsistency. Under AU-C 720, the report should:
choices: Include a separate section titled 'Other Information' describing management's responsibility and the auditor's responsibility and conclusion
Contain an opinion on the other information
Include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph on the other information
Omit any reference to the other information
questions.exp: AU-C 720 (SAS 137) requires a separate 'Other Information' section when the annual report contains other information, stating that the auditor does not express an opinion on it and describing the result of reading it. No opinion is expressed on other information.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer audits financial statements prepared on the cash basis of accounting. Under AU-C 800, the auditor's report should include:
choices: An adverse opinion because the statements depart from GAAP
A qualified opinion
A restriction on use paragraph for all cash basis reports
An emphasis-of-matter paragraph alerting users to the basis of accounting and stating that it is a basis other than GAAP
questions.exp: AU-C 800 requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that refers to the note describing the special purpose framework. Restricted use is required for contractual and regulatory bases, not for cash or tax basis, and no modification is needed because GAAP is not the applicable framework.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct date for an auditor's report on a nonissuer?
choices: The date the auditor began fieldwork
The date the financial statements are issued to users

No earlier than the date on which the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence, including evidence that the financial statements were prepared and that those with authority have asserted responsibility for them
The date of the balance sheet
questions.exp: AU-C 700 requires the report to be dated no earlier than when sufficient appropriate evidence is obtained, including evidence that the statements, including disclosures, have been prepared and management has asserted responsibility. Issuance may occur later than the report date.

questions.q: An auditor concludes that a nonissuer failed to consolidate a material subsidiary, and the effects are both material and pervasive. The auditor should express:
choices: An adverse opinion
An unmodified opinion with an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
A qualified opinion
A disclaimer of opinion
questions.exp: A material and pervasive misstatement, such as failure to consolidate, results in an adverse opinion under AU-C 705. A disclaimer is for scope limitations, and a qualified opinion is for misstatements that are not pervasive.

questions.q: In an adverse opinion on a nonissuer's financial statements, the auditor's report should:
choices: State that the auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence
Omit the basis section
Express an unmodified opinion on the balance sheet and adverse opinion on the income statement as piecemeal opinions
Include a 'Basis for Adverse Opinion' section describing the matter and, if practicable, quantifying its effects
questions.exp: AU-C 705 requires a Basis for Adverse Opinion section describing and quantifying the misstatement if practicable. Piecemeal opinions are not permitted with an adverse opinion on the statements as a whole, and inability to obtain evidence relates to disclaimers.

questions.q: The auditor of a nonissuer is also engaged to report on supplementary schedules of operating expenses accompanying the financial statements. Under AU-C 725, the auditor's report on the schedules most typically states that:
choices: The information was compiled from management's records
The information is presented fairly in accordance with GAAP as a standalone statement
The auditor applied limited procedures and expresses no opinion
The information is fairly stated, in all material respects, in relation to the financial statements as a whole
questions.exp: Under AU-C 725, the auditor reports whether supplementary information is fairly stated in relation to the financial statements as a whole. Limited procedures and no opinion describe RSI under AU-C 730.

questions.q: A nonissuer's prior-year financial statements were restated to correct a material misstatement, and the restatement is properly disclosed. In the current-year report on comparative statements, the auditor should:
choices: Include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph regarding the correction of the misstatement
Issue a disclaimer on the prior year
Make no reference to the restatement
Issue a qualified opinion on the prior year
questions.exp: AU-C 708 requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph for a correction of a material misstatement in previously issued financial statements. The restated statements are fairly presented, so no qualification is needed.

questions.q: Under AU-C 705, the term 'pervasive' describes effects on the financial statements that:
choices: Exceed overall materiality by any amount
Relate to fraud involving senior management
Are not confined to specific elements, or if confined represent a substantial proportion of the statements, or relate to disclosures fundamental to users' understanding
Relate to a single account balance that is large
questions.exp: AU-C 705 defines pervasive effects as those not confined to specific elements, accounts, or items, or if confined, representing a substantial proportion of the statements, or disclosures fundamental to understanding. Exceeding materiality alone makes something material, not pervasive.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer identifies a matter that is appropriately disclosed and is of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements. The auditor is not engaged to report KAMs. The auditor may:
choices: Disclose additional facts not included in the financial statements
Include an emphasis-of-matter paragraph that refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements
Include an other-matter paragraph
Qualify the opinion
questions.exp: AU-C 706 permits an emphasis-of-matter paragraph for appropriately disclosed matters fundamental to users' understanding, and it may refer only to information presented or disclosed. The auditor does not provide original information about the entity, and no qualification applies when no misstatement exists.

questions.q: A nonissuer prepares financial statements in accordance with a contractual basis of accounting for use by a lender. Under AU-C 800, which is required?
choices: An adverse opinion for departure from GAAP
A statement that the financial statements comply with GAAP
A disclaimer of opinion
An other-matter paragraph restricting the use of the report to the specified parties
questions.exp: AU-C 800 requires a restricted-use alert in an other-matter paragraph when statements are prepared under a contractual or regulatory basis of accounting. Special purpose frameworks are not departures from GAAP requiring modification.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer engaged to communicate KAMs determines that a significant matter is fundamental to users' understanding and is also a KAM. Which is most appropriate?
choices: Include it as both an emphasis-of-matter paragraph and a KAM, repeating the same text
Exclude it from the report entirely
Qualify the opinion on the matter
Communicate it in the KAM section, which may highlight its relative importance, rather than also in an emphasis-of-matter paragraph
questions.exp: AU-C 706 states that an emphasis-of-matter paragraph is not a substitute for a KAM, and when a matter is determined to be a KAM, the auditor generally communicates it in the KAM section rather than in a separate emphasis-of-matter paragraph. No qualification is warranted for an appropriately presented matter.

questions.q: When a predecessor auditor's report on prior-period comparative statements is not reissued, the successor auditor's report should include an other-matter paragraph stating:
choices: That the prior-period statements were audited by another auditor, the type of opinion and date of that report, and the reasons for any modification
That the successor assumes responsibility for the predecessor's work
The name of the predecessor auditor in all cases
That the successor reaudited the prior period
questions.exp: AU-C 700 requires an other-matter paragraph indicating that a predecessor audited the prior period, the date and type of opinion, and reasons for any modification. The predecessor is generally not named, and the successor does not assume responsibility for the predecessor's work.

questions.q: A nonissuer auditor issues a qualified opinion due to an inability to observe beginning inventory. Which wording is consistent with the qualified opinion?
choices: 'The financial statements do not present fairly'
'Except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the financial statements present fairly...'
'Because of the significance of the matter, we do not express an opinion'
'Except for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the financial statements present fairly...'
questions.exp: When qualifying due to a scope limitation, AU-C 705 uses 'except for the possible effects,' because the auditor has not determined that a misstatement exists. 'Except for the effects' is used for actual misstatements.

questions.q: An auditor of a nonissuer becomes aware, after the report date but before release, that management materially revised a disclosure. Which is most appropriate?
choices: Extend subsequent-event procedures to the new date and either dual-date or redate the report as applicable
Withdraw from the engagement
Issue an adverse opinion
Release the report with the original date and no further procedures
questions.exp: When financial statements are amended after the report date, AU-C 560 requires the auditor to perform procedures on the amendment and either dual-date (limiting procedures to the amendment) or redate the report (extending procedures). Releasing without considering the change is inappropriate.

questions.q: An auditor's report on a nonissuer includes an emphasis-of-matter paragraph. Which statement about that paragraph is accurate?
choices: It modifies the auditor's opinion
It is used to describe misstatements that management refused to correct
It must be placed before the Opinion section
It must include a statement that the auditor's opinion is not modified with respect to the matter
questions.exp: AU-C 706 requires an emphasis-of-matter paragraph to state that the opinion is not modified with respect to the matter emphasized. It is not a modification, and misstatements require a modified opinion.

questions.q: An auditor sets planned audit risk at 5% for an assertion, assesses inherent risk at 80%, and assesses control risk at 50%. Using the audit risk model, what is the acceptable level of detection risk?
questions.exp: Detection risk = AR / (IR x CR) = 0.05 / (0.80 x 0.50) = 0.05 / 0.40 = 12.5%. Dividing by inherent risk alone gives 6.25%, and multiplying all three factors gives 2%.

questions.q: Tests of controls over purchasing reveal more deviations than expected, so the auditor raises the assessed control risk for the completeness of accounts payable. Which response is most appropriate?
choices: Lower the assessed inherent risk to offset the higher control risk
Leave detection risk unchanged, because control risk does not affect substantive procedures
Increase acceptable detection risk and reduce the extent of substantive tests
Decrease acceptable detection risk, for example by performing more extensive substantive procedures at year-end rather than at an interim date
questions.exp: Detection risk moves inversely with the RMM. Higher control risk means acceptable detection risk must fall, so the auditor needs more persuasive substantive evidence through changes in nature, timing toward period-end, or extent. Inherent risk is assessed independently and cannot be lowered to offset control risk.

questions.q: After performing risk assessment procedures, an auditor concludes that both inherent risk and control risk for the valuation of inventory are higher than in the prior year. Which component of audit risk can the auditor directly change in response?
choices: Control risk, by recommending improvements to management
Detection risk, by changing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures
Inherent risk, by modifying the audit approach to inventory
The risk of material misstatement, by lowering performance materiality
questions.exp: Inherent and control risk are characteristics of the entity that exist whether or not there is an audit. The auditor assesses them but does not control them. The auditor manages detection risk through the substantive procedures it designs and performs.

questions.q: Under AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145, an auditor does not plan to test the operating effectiveness of controls over an assertion. How should the auditor assess the risk of material misstatement for that assertion?
choices: Assess the RMM as a single combined risk, without separately assessing inherent risk
Assess control risk based on the design of controls evaluated during walkthroughs
Assess control risk at a low level if no deficiencies were identified in the prior year
Assess inherent risk separately and assess control risk at the maximum, so that the RMM equals the assessed inherent risk
questions.exp: SAS No. 145 requires separate assessments of inherent risk and control risk at the assertion level. If the auditor does not plan to test operating effectiveness, control risk is assessed at the maximum, so the RMM is the inherent risk assessment. Design evaluation alone cannot support a lower control risk.

questions.q: Which of the following risks must the auditor treat as a significant risk?
choices: An assessed risk of material misstatement due to fraud
The risk related to processing routine, high-volume cash receipts
Any risk in an account whose balance exceeds performance materiality
Any risk for which control risk is assessed at the maximum
questions.exp: AU-C 240 requires the auditor to treat assessed risks of material misstatement due to fraud as significant risks. Routine, high-volume processing is usually lower in inherent risk, and neither account size nor maximum control risk alone makes a risk significant.

questions.q: An auditor plans to respond to a significant risk related to the valuation of complex derivative instruments using only substantive procedures. Under AU-C 330, those procedures must include
choices: substantive analytical procedures, which are alone sufficient
tests of details
a review of the prior-year working papers for the same risk
inquiries of the treasury department and review of board minutes
questions.exp: When the approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, AU-C 330 requires those procedures to include tests of details. Substantive analytical procedures alone are not sufficient for a significant risk.

questions.q: An auditor uses 5% of pretax income from continuing operations as the benchmark for materiality and sets performance materiality at 75% of overall materiality. Pretax income from continuing operations is $2,400,000. What is performance materiality?
questions.exp: Overall materiality = 5% x $2,400,000 = $120,000, and performance materiality = 75% x $120,000 = $90,000. The $120,000 figure is overall materiality, which is the common mistake of stopping one step early.

questions.q: An auditor sets overall materiality at 1% of total assets of $40,000,000 and sets the clearly trivial threshold at 5% of overall materiality. Misstatements below what amount need not be accumulated?
questions.exp: Overall materiality is 1% x $40,000,000 = $400,000, and clearly trivial is 5% x $400,000 = $20,000. Under AU-C 450, misstatements that are clearly trivial need not be accumulated. Using $400,000 confuses materiality with the much smaller clearly trivial threshold.

questions.q: An auditor based preliminary materiality on forecast pretax income of $5,000,000. Late in the audit, actual pretax income is determined to be only $3,000,000. Under AU-C 320, the auditor should
choices: retain the preliminary materiality, because materiality is fixed once the audit plan is approved
revise materiality and determine whether performance materiality and the nature, timing, and extent of further audit procedures remain appropriate
revise materiality only if management agrees to the revision
increase materiality to reflect the greater uncertainty in the results
questions.exp: AU-C 320 requires the auditor to revise materiality when information becomes known that would have led to a different amount initially. A lower materiality may require more audit work. Materiality is not fixed at planning, and management's agreement is irrelevant.

questions.q: Under AU-C 320, when is it appropriate to set a materiality level lower than overall materiality for particular classes of transactions, account balances, or disclosures?
choices: When the account is too large for the auditor to test completely
When the auditor wants to reduce the sample sizes for those accounts
When misstatements of smaller amounts could reasonably be expected to influence users' decisions, as with related party transactions or key management compensation
When management requests additional assurance on specific accounts
questions.exp: Specific materiality applies when law, regulation, the framework, or users' expectations make smaller misstatements in particular items influential, such as related party transactions, executive compensation, or industry-specific disclosures. A lower materiality increases testing, so it would never be used to reduce sample sizes.

questions.q: Overall materiality is $100,000. Which of the following uncorrected misstatements would most likely be considered material despite being below that amount?
choices: A $70,000 overstatement of accounts payable offset by an equal overstatement of inventory
A $40,000 overstatement of income that causes the company to meet a debt covenant it would otherwise have violated
A $40,000 understatement of a prepaid insurance balance that has no effect on any covenant
A $60,000 classification error between two operating expense lines
questions.exp: Qualitative factors under AU-C 450, such as the effect on compliance with debt covenants, can make a quantitatively small misstatement material. Misclassifications within operating expenses generally have little effect on users' decisions.

questions.q: At the end of an audit, the auditor has identified uncorrected factual misstatements of $25,000, a $15,000 difference between management's estimate and the auditor's estimate, and projected misstatements from sampling, net of the factual misstatements found in the samples, of $40,000. All of these overstate income. What total amount should the auditor compare with materiality?
questions.exp: AU-C 450 requires the auditor to evaluate the aggregate of factual, judgmental, and projected misstatements: $25,000 + $15,000 + $40,000 = $80,000. Leaving out either the judgmental or the projected misstatements understates the likely misstatement.

questions.q: Management recorded an allowance for credit losses of $500,000. The auditor developed a range of reasonable outcomes from $420,000 to $470,000 and concluded that the range is supported by sufficient appropriate evidence. What is the misstatement in the allowance?
choices: $0, because the auditor's range is reasonable
questions.exp: When management's point estimate is outside the auditor's reasonable range, the misstatement is at least the difference between management's estimate and the nearest point of the range: $500,000 - $470,000 = $30,000. Measuring to the low end of the range or to its midpoint overstates the misstatement.

questions.q: Regarding uncorrected misstatements, the written representations the auditor obtains from management should include
choices: management's belief that the effects of uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, individually and in aggregate, with a summary of the items included in or attached to the letter
the auditor's calculation of projected misstatements for each sample
a statement that the auditor agrees with management's assessment of each misstatement
a statement that management will correct the misstatements in the next fiscal year
questions.exp: AU-C 580 and AU-C 450 require management to represent that it believes the effects of uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, individually and in aggregate, with a summary of those items included or attached. The representation is management's, not the auditor's, and does not promise future correction.

questions.q: Under AU-C 450, which misstatements should the auditor request management to correct?
choices: Only misstatements that individually exceed performance materiality
Only factual misstatements, because judgmental misstatements are a matter of opinion
Only misstatements that individually exceed overall materiality
All misstatements accumulated during the audit, other than those that are clearly trivial
questions.exp: AU-C 450 requires the auditor to communicate all accumulated misstatements on a timely basis and to request that management correct them, not just those above materiality. Only clearly trivial items are excluded from accumulation. Judgmental misstatements are included as well.

questions.q: Which of the following is an inherent risk factor as described in AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145?
choices: Ineffective general IT controls over access to programs
The auditor's lack of experience in the client's industry
Subjectivity in measuring an accounting estimate
The sample size the auditor plans to use for tests of details
questions.exp: SAS No. 145 identifies inherent risk factors as complexity, subjectivity, change, uncertainty, and susceptibility to misstatement from management bias or fraud. Ineffective IT general controls relate to control risk, and sample size relates to detection risk.

questions.q: During risk assessment, the auditor identifies significant deficiencies in the control environment, including management's weak commitment to competent financial reporting staff. Which overall response to this financial statement-level risk is most appropriate?
choices: Assess control risk below the maximum to offset the weak control environment
Reduce the involvement of experienced staff so that procedures are performed independently of management
Perform more audit procedures as of the period end rather than at an interim date
Perform more substantive procedures at interim dates to spread the work evenly
questions.exp: AU-C 330 says that a weak control environment may call for overall responses, such as performing more procedures at period-end, obtaining more extensive evidence, assigning more experienced staff, increasing supervision, and adding unpredictability. Relying more on interim work assumes controls carry the results forward to period-end, which a weak environment does not support.

questions.q: In which situation would an auditor most likely set performance materiality at a lower percentage of overall materiality?
choices: The entity's accounts are few and individually large
The client has a history of numerous misstatements identified in prior audits
The auditor plans to rely on controls that were effective in prior years
The client has stable operations and no misstatements were identified in prior audits
questions.exp: Performance materiality reduces the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements together exceed materiality. Expecting more misstatements, based on history, calls for a lower performance materiality. A clean history and effective controls support a higher percentage.

questions.q: A company's pretax income has fluctuated between small losses and small profits over the past five years, while revenues have been stable at about $50,000,000. Which benchmark is most likely appropriate for overall materiality?
choices: The smallest account balance in the trial balance
Current-year pretax income, because it is always the preferred benchmark for for-profit entities
Total revenues or a normalized earnings measure rather than current-year pretax income
Total liabilities, because creditors are the primary users
questions.exp: AU-C 320 guidance notes that when profit is volatile or near breakeven, a stable benchmark such as revenues or normalized earnings may be more appropriate. Using a near-zero pretax income would produce an unrealistically low materiality.

questions.q: In an audit performed under PCAOB standards, AS 2105 requires that tolerable misstatement for an individual account or disclosure be
choices: less than materiality for the financial statements as a whole
determined by applying a fixed percentage of the account's balance
equal to materiality for the financial statements as a whole
approved by the audit committee before fieldwork begins
questions.exp: AS 2105 requires tolerable misstatement at the account or disclosure level to be less than materiality for the financial statements as a whole, so that the misstatements across accounts are not material in total. No fixed percentage is prescribed, and the audit committee does not approve it.

questions.q: Which of the following is most likely to reduce nonsampling risk in an audit?
choices: Increasing sample sizes for tests of details
Using statistical rather than nonstatistical sampling methods
Proper planning, supervision, and review of the engagement team's work
Increasing tolerable misstatement for the accounts tested
questions.exp: Nonsampling risk comes from inappropriate procedures or misinterpreted evidence and is reduced by planning, supervision, review, and quality management. Larger samples and statistical methods address sampling risk instead.

questions.q: Holding audit risk constant, an auditor reduces overall materiality because the financial statements will be used in connection with a proposed sale of the company. The most likely effect is that
choices: the assessed inherent risk will decrease
more audit evidence is needed, such as larger sample sizes for tests of details
detection risk will increase
less audit evidence is needed, because users will be more knowledgeable
questions.exp: Materiality and the amount of evidence are inversely related. A lower materiality requires more evidence so the auditor can detect smaller misstatements. It does not change inherent risk, and detection risk must decrease, not increase.

questions.q: In a group audit, the group auditor determines materiality to be used for the work on a significant component. That materiality should be
choices: lower than materiality for the group financial statements as a whole, to reduce aggregation risk
higher than group materiality, because each component is smaller than the group
equal to materiality for the group financial statements for every component, so results are comparable
set by component management and accepted by the group auditor
questions.exp: Under AU-C 600, materiality for work at components is set below group materiality so that the probability of the aggregate of misstatements across components exceeding group materiality is acceptably low. Using group materiality at each component ignores aggregation risk.

questions.q: A company's senior executives receive large bonuses only if earnings per share meet aggressive targets that analysts consider unlikely. In the fraud triangle described in AU-C 240, this circumstance is primarily an example of
choices: a weakness in the monitoring component of internal control
an incentive or pressure to commit fraud
an opportunity to commit fraud
an attitude or rationalization
questions.exp: Compensation tied to aggressive targets creates an incentive or pressure for fraudulent financial reporting. Opportunity relates to weak controls or complex transactions, and attitude relates to management's willingness to justify dishonest acts.

questions.q: Ending inventory in the prior year was overstated by $30,000, and the misstatement was not corrected. In the current year, the auditor identifies an uncorrected $50,000 overstatement of current-year revenue. Considering both items, what is the net effect on current-year pretax income?
choices: $20,000 overstatement
$50,000 overstatement
$20,000 understatement
$80,000 overstatement
questions.exp: The prior-year overstatement of ending inventory overstates current-year beginning inventory and cost of sales, understating current income by $30,000. Combined with the $50,000 revenue overstatement, the net effect is a $20,000 overstatement. Adding the two amounts ignores that the inventory error reverses in the current year.

questions.q: Under AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145, an assertion is a relevant assertion when
choices: management has designed controls over the assertion
it has an identified risk of material misstatement, meaning there is a reasonable possibility of a misstatement occurring that could be material
the auditor intends to rely on controls related to the assertion
the related account balance exceeds overall materiality
questions.exp: SAS No. 145 defines a relevant assertion as one with an identified RMM, which exists when a misstatement is reasonably possible and could be material. Account size alone does not make an assertion relevant, and relevance does not depend on whether controls exist or will be relied on.

questions.q: An auditor assesses the risk of material misstatement as low for all assertions related to a material prepaid expenses balance. Under AU-C 330, the auditor
choices: should test controls over prepaid expenses instead of performing substantive procedures
may omit substantive procedures for the balance, because the RMM is low
may rely solely on inquiry of management about the balance
should still design and perform substantive procedures for the material account balance
questions.exp: AU-C 330 requires substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance, and disclosure regardless of the assessed RMM. This reflects the judgmental nature of risk assessment and the inherent limitations of internal control. Inquiry alone is never sufficient.

questions.q: A retailer initiates, records, and processes most of its sales electronically with no manual intervention or documentation outside the IT system. For the occurrence and completeness of sales, the auditor most likely will need to
choices: rely on management's representations about the system's reliability
test the operating effectiveness of relevant controls, because substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate evidence
perform only substantive analytical procedures on sales
vouch a large sample of sales to paper shipping documents
questions.exp: AU-C 315 and AU-C 330 recognize that when transactions are processed in highly automated systems with little documentation outside the system, substantive procedures alone may not be sufficient, so the auditor must test controls. Paper documents may not exist, and representations do not substitute for evidence.

questions.q: Under AU-C 320, which of the following must the auditor include in the audit documentation regarding materiality?
choices: Materiality for the financial statements as a whole, any lower specific materiality levels, performance materiality, the factors considered in determining them, and any revisions
Only the final materiality amount used at the end of the audit
Management's approval of the materiality amounts
The materiality amounts used by other firms auditing companies in the same industry
questions.exp: AU-C 320 requires documentation of overall materiality, any specific materiality levels, performance materiality, the factors considered, and any revisions as the audit progressed. Management does not approve the auditor's materiality judgments.

questions.q: For one assertion, the auditor assesses inherent risk as high and, after testing operating effectiveness, control risk as low. For a second assertion, both inherent risk and control risk are high. Compared with the second assertion, the acceptable detection risk for the first assertion is
choices: higher, so less persuasive substantive evidence may be sufficient
the same, because inherent risk is high for both
zero, because effective controls replace substantive procedures
lower, so the auditor must perform more extensive substantive tests
questions.exp: Effective controls lower the RMM for the first assertion, which permits higher acceptable detection risk and less persuasive or less extensive substantive procedures than when both risks are high. Detection risk can never be zero, because substantive procedures are always required for material items.

questions.q: In planning a statistical attribute sample for a test of controls, which change, with all other factors held constant, would increase the required sample size?
choices: A decrease in the tolerable deviation rate from 7% to 4%
An increase in the population size from 20,000 to 60,000 items
A decrease in the expected population deviation rate from 2% to 1%
An increase in the acceptable risk of overreliance from 5% to 10%
questions.exp: Sample size is inversely related to the tolerable deviation rate, so a lower tolerable rate requires a larger sample. A higher acceptable risk of overreliance and a lower expected deviation rate both reduce sample size, and population size has little effect once the population is large.

questions.q: Based on prior-year results, an auditor raises the expected population deviation rate for a control from 1% to 2.5%, holding the tolerable rate at 6% and the risk of overreliance at 5%. The required sample size will
choices: decrease to zero, because the control should not be relied on
decrease, because more deviations are expected
increase, because a larger sample is needed to show that the true rate does not exceed the tolerable rate
stay the same, because the tolerable rate did not change
questions.exp: As the expected deviation rate approaches the tolerable rate, a larger sample is needed to conclude with the desired confidence that the true rate does not exceed the tolerable rate. Expecting more deviations does not mean the control can no longer be relied on.

questions.q: In substantive tests of details, which aspect of sampling risk relates primarily to audit efficiency rather than audit effectiveness?
choices: The risk of incorrect rejection
The risk of incorrect acceptance
Nonsampling risk
The risk of overreliance on controls
questions.exp: The risk of incorrect rejection leads the auditor to conclude that a fairly stated balance is misstated, which usually results in more work rather than a wrong opinion, so it is an efficiency risk. The risk of incorrect acceptance and the risk of overreliance affect effectiveness because they could lead to an inappropriate opinion.

questions.q: An auditor tests a control using a statistical sample of 100 items with a 5% risk of overreliance and a tolerable deviation rate of 6%. Three deviations are found, and the statistical table gives an upper deviation limit of 7.6%. What is the allowance for sampling risk, and what should the auditor conclude?
choices: 1.6%; the control can be relied on with a slight increase in substantive testing
3.0%; the control can be relied on as planned because the sample deviation rate is below the tolerable rate
4.6%; the control cannot be relied on as planned because the upper deviation limit exceeds the tolerable rate
7.6%; the control cannot be relied on, because any deviation means the control is ineffective
questions.exp: The sample deviation rate is 3/100 = 3%, and the allowance for sampling risk is 7.6% - 3.0% = 4.6%. The upper limit, not the sample rate, is compared with the tolerable rate. Because 7.6% exceeds 6%, the auditor cannot rely on the control as planned and should adjust the substantive procedures.

questions.q: An auditor examines a sample of 80 purchase orders for proper approval and finds 2 deviations. The tolerable deviation rate is 8%, and the statistical table gives an upper deviation limit of 7.6% at the planned risk of overreliance. Which conclusion is appropriate?
choices: The sample deviation rate of 2.5% exceeds the expected rate, so the control cannot be relied on
The control cannot be relied on, because the upper deviation limit exceeds the sample deviation rate
The sample results support relying on the control as planned, because the 7.6% upper deviation limit does not exceed the 8% tolerable rate
The auditor must expand the sample, because any deviations prevent a conclusion
questions.exp: The decision rule compares the upper deviation limit (sample rate of 2/80 = 2.5% plus the allowance for sampling risk) with the tolerable rate. Because 7.6% is below 8%, the results support reliance. The upper limit always exceeds the sample rate, so that comparison means nothing.

questions.q: An auditor suspects that fictitious vendors may have been added to the vendor master file. The auditor wants to design a sample with a high probability of finding at least one fictitious vendor if the rate is at or above a very low critical level. Which sampling plan is most appropriate?
choices: Discovery sampling
Ratio estimation
Stop-or-go sampling for a routine control
Mean-per-unit estimation
questions.exp: Discovery sampling is a form of attribute sampling used when the expected rate is near zero and even one occurrence, such as fraud, would be critical. Ratio and mean-per-unit estimation are variables methods that estimate dollar amounts.

questions.q: Which statement best describes sequential (stop-or-go) sampling in tests of controls?
choices: The sample is selected in stages, and whether more items are examined depends on the results of the earlier stages
The population is divided into strata, and each stratum is sampled separately
Every nth item is selected after a random start
Items are selected in proportion to their dollar amounts
questions.exp: In sequential sampling, the auditor examines an initial sample and, depending on the deviations found, either stops or expands the sample. This can reduce sample sizes when few deviations are found. Selecting every nth item is systematic selection, and selecting in proportion to dollars is MUS.

questions.q: Using monetary unit sampling with no expected misstatement, an auditor tests accounts receivable with a recorded balance of $500,000. Tolerable misstatement is $25,000, and the reliability factor for zero misstatements at the desired risk of incorrect acceptance is 3.0. What is the sample size?
questions.exp: The sampling interval is $25,000 / 3.0 = $8,333, and the sample size is $500,000 / $8,333 = 60, which is the same as ($500,000 x 3.0) / $25,000. The $8,333 figure is the sampling interval, not the sample size.

questions.q: An auditor uses monetary unit sampling for inventory with a recorded amount of $600,000. Tolerable misstatement is $30,000, expected misstatement is $5,000, the reliability factor is 3.0, and the expansion factor is 1.6. What is the required sample size, rounded up?
questions.exp: Sample size = (BV x RF) / (TM - EM x expansion factor) = ($600,000 x 3.0) / ($30,000 - $8,000) = $1,800,000 / $22,000 = 81.8, which rounds up to 82. Ignoring the expected misstatement gives 60, and leaving out the expansion factor gives 72.

questions.q: In a monetary unit sample with a sampling interval of $10,000, the auditor finds two misstatements. One account recorded at $2,000 has an audited value of $1,500. Another account recorded at $15,000 has an audited value of $12,000. What is the total projected misstatement?
choices: $5,500 understatement
$5,500 overstatement
questions.exp: For the $2,000 item, which is smaller than the interval, the tainting is $500 / $2,000 = 25%, and the projection is 25% x $10,000 = $2,500. The $15,000 item is larger than the interval, so its actual $3,000 misstatement is used without projection. The total is $5,500 overstatement. Adding only the actual differences gives $3,500.

questions.q: In a monetary unit sample, basic precision is $30,000, total projected misstatement is $5,500, and the incremental allowance for sampling risk is $1,875. Tolerable misstatement is $40,000. What is the upper limit on misstatement, and what should the auditor conclude?
choices: $7,375; the balance is accepted because projected misstatement is less than tolerable misstatement
$35,500; the balance should be adjusted by the full upper limit
$37,375; the results support the conclusion that the balance is not misstated by more than tolerable misstatement
$37,375; the balance must be rejected because the upper limit exceeds basic precision
questions.exp: The upper misstatement limit is basic precision + projected misstatement + incremental allowance = $30,000 + $5,500 + $1,875 = $37,375. Because it is below the $40,000 tolerable misstatement, the results support acceptance. The upper limit always exceeds basic precision when misstatements are found.

questions.q: Monetary unit sampling would be least appropriate when the auditor's primary objective is to
choices: test accounts receivable for overstatement
test a population in which each item has a recorded dollar amount
test accounts payable for understatement, including vendor accounts with zero recorded balances
test a population in which few misstatements are expected
questions.exp: MUS selects items in proportion to their recorded amounts, so understated items have less chance of selection and zero-balance items cannot be selected. It is well suited to testing overstatement in populations with few expected misstatements.

questions.q: In a monetary unit sampling application with a sampling interval of $12,000, which customer account is certain to be selected?
choices: Any account that was misstated in the prior year
Any account with a recorded balance of $12,000 or more
Any account with a balance between $6,000 and $12,000
The first account listed in the population
questions.exp: With systematic selection of dollar units, any logical unit equal to or larger than the sampling interval contains at least one selected dollar and is certain to be selected. This automatic stratification is an advantage of MUS. Smaller balances have only a probability of selection proportional to their size.

questions.q: Using mean-per-unit estimation, an auditor selects a sample from a population of 5,000 inventory items. The average audited value of the sample items is $410. What is the estimated audited value of the population?
questions.exp: Mean-per-unit estimation multiplies the average audited value per sample item by the number of items in the population: $410 x 5,000 = $2,050,000. The estimate is then compared with the recorded amount and evaluated using the allowance for sampling risk.

questions.q: Using ratio estimation, an auditor selects a sample of accounts receivable with a total recorded amount of $50,000 and a total audited amount of $49,000. The population's recorded amount is $2,000,000. What is the projected misstatement?
choices: $40,000 overstatement
$20,000 overstatement
$1,000 overstatement
$40,000 understatement
questions.exp: The ratio of audited to recorded amount is $49,000 / $50,000 = 0.98, so the estimated audited value is 0.98 x $2,000,000 = $1,960,000. That implies a $40,000 overstatement. The $1,000 is only the sample difference, not the projection.

questions.q: Using difference estimation, an auditor selects 200 items from a population of 4,000 vouchers with a recorded amount of $2,000,000. The total net difference in the sample is $1,000, with recorded amounts exceeding audited amounts. What is the projected misstatement for the population?
choices: $10,000 overstatement
$1,000 overstatement
$20,000 understatement
$20,000 overstatement
questions.exp: The average difference per item is $1,000 / 200 = $5, and $5 x 4,000 items = $20,000. Because recorded amounts exceed audited amounts, the population is overstated. Reporting only the $1,000 sample difference ignores the projection.

questions.q: Ratio and difference estimation are generally most appropriate when
choices: few or no misstatements are expected and the main concern is overstatement
the auditor wants a sample size that is unaffected by population variability
many differences between recorded and audited amounts are expected and the differences are not highly skewed
the population contains no recorded book values for individual items
questions.exp: Ratio and difference estimation need enough differences in the sample to produce reliable estimates, so they work best when many differences are expected. MUS is more efficient when few misstatements are expected. Both methods require book values, and variability affects classical sample sizes.

questions.q: When using classical variables sampling, an auditor stratifies an accounts receivable population into high-dollar and low-dollar groups. The primary benefit is that stratification
choices: allows the auditor to ignore the low-dollar stratum
converts the sample into a monetary unit sample
eliminates the need to project misstatements
reduces the variability within each stratum, allowing a smaller total sample size for the same precision and confidence
questions.exp: Classical variables sample sizes depend heavily on the standard deviation of the population. Stratifying into more uniform groups reduces variability and therefore the required sample size. Misstatements must still be projected for each stratum, and no stratum may be ignored.

questions.q: Which sample selection method is acceptable for nonstatistical sampling but is not appropriate when statistical sampling is used?
choices: Systematic selection with a random start
Haphazard selection
Random selection
Selection with probability proportional to size
questions.exp: AU-C 530 permits haphazard selection, which is selection without a conscious bias or predictable pattern, for nonstatistical samples. Statistical sampling requires selection methods with known, calculable probabilities, such as random, systematic with a random start, or PPS selection.

questions.q: An inventory population of $2,000,000 includes 10 key items totaling $500,000 that the auditor tests 100%, finding misstatements of $5,000. The remaining $1,500,000 is sampled nonstatistically. Sample items with a recorded amount of $100,000 contain misstatements of $2,000.
